text: Robert Patrick Weston (né Harris; 7 March 1878 – 6 November 1936) was an English songwriter known for his numerous successful songs and comic monologues between the 1900s and 1930s, primarily written in collaboration with other writers, notably Fred J. Barnes and Bert Lee, and performed by Harry Champion, Stanley Holloway, and Gracie Fields, among others. Born in Kingsbury Road, Islington, near Dalston Junction in London, his father operated a grocery shop, and the family lived above it. Harris initially worked for an engineering company but was dismissed for spending time writing verses on the back of scraps of emery paper. He married Maud Barker in 1900 and became a railway clerk, living in Hemmingford Road, Islington, before taking up performing and songwriting. For his wife's health, they moved to Weston-super-Mare, where Harris joined a concert party, adopted the stage name Weston, and formed the double act Conway and Weston. He later moved to Ramsgate, where he began writing songs, before returning to London. He sold his first song, "Boys of the Chelsea School," to the publishing firm Francis, Day and Hunter in 1902, popularised by George Leyton. Among his most successful early works were "What a Mouth," sung by Harry Champion in 1906 and revived in 1960 by Tommy Steele; and "I'm Henery the Eighth, I Am," written with Fred Murray in 1910 and first recorded by Champion, which reached number one on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1965 with Herman's Hermits. Weston had a successful partnership with Fred J. Barnes, co-writing "Little Willie's Woodbines" (1908), "I've Got Rings On My Fingers" (1909), "When Father Papered the Parlour" (1910, popularised by Billy Williams), and "Hush Here Comes the Dream Man" (1911, recorded by Florrie Forde, parodied by First World War soldiers as "Hush Here Comes a Whizzbang," and performed in the 1963 Theatre Workshop production of Oh, What a Lovely War!). He also co-wrote "Sister Susie's Sewing Shirts for Soldiers" with Herman Darewski in 1914, which became Al Jolson's first hit. In 1915, music publisher David Day of Francis, Day and Hunter introduced him to Bert Lee, with whom he had the most enduring collaboration. Over the next twenty years, they produced around 3000 songs and monologues, 75 stage shows and musicals, and 17 films, as well as pantomimes and radio shows, writing in Weston's Twickenham home with daily meetings and a goal of creating at least one song per day. Both composed both lyrics and music, though Lee noted, "Bob has the brains. I put the laughs in." Their work included revues produced by Lupino Lane and sketches for performers such as Fred Karno, Robb Wilton, and Wee Georgie Wood. In the 1920s, they adapted American productions for the British stage and began working with producers Jack Waller and Joe Tunbridge in 1926, writing several musical comedies featuring comedian Bobby Howes, including the monologue "My Word, You Do Look Queer," first recorded by Ernest Hastings in 1922 and later popularised by Stanley Holloway. They also wrote sketches for the Crazy Gang and many of Stanley Holloway's monologues in the 1930s. Together with his son Harris Weston (born Robert Edgar Harris, 1901–1978), they co-wrote Holloway's 1934 monologue "With Her Head Tucked Underneath Her Arm," about the ghost of Anne Boleyn haunting the Tower of London seeking revenge on Henry VIII, and also created Gracie Fields' 1933 song "Heaven Will Protect an Honest Girl" and the 1936 piece "Harmonica Dan." Weston was also an amateur artist whose works reflect his London background, including a 1916 watercolour of Houndsditch Market. He died from a brain tumour in London in 1936 at the age of 58. After his death, his house in Twickenham was occupied by his two daughters, who lived there into old age, and Weston and Lee's papers remained untouched. Several of their items have appeared on eBay, including a three-volume workbook containing manuscript versions of many, if not all, their songs, now held by a collector of music hall memorabilia. In 1985, entertainer Roy Hudd created a stage show, Just a Verse and a Chorus, based on the songs of Weston and Lee, performed by Hudd and Billy Dainty, and wrote about them in the now-defunct periodical Theatrephile. Hudd also adapted the show into a series for BBC Radio 2. A programme on Weston and Lee's lives and work was broadcast on BBC Radio 4 on 16 June 2009, presented by Children's Laureate Michael Rosen.
